1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 49-year-old middle-aged woman who has worked in farming at home for many years. She was admitted through the emergency department on Day 0, for "recurrent fever, productive cough, dyspnea for more than 50 days, and mechanical ventilation for half a month." During the history-taking process, it was learned that the patient had previously been healthy. She developed cough, sputum production, and dyspnea at onset, followed by fever. After anti-infective treatment and repeated intubations, she ultimately underwent tracheostomy for respiratory support, but not only did her condition fail to improve, it progressively worsened. She had also been sent to a local psychiatric hospital for treatment because of psychiatric symptoms such as incoherent speech. On Day -57, after catching a cold, the patient developed cough, thick yellow sticky sputum, dyspnea, and fatigue. She received IV "anti-inflammatory medication" (details unknown) at a local clinic for more than 10 days, but her original symptoms further worsened, and she developed fever with a maximum temperature of 39℃, without chills. On Day -42, the patient was hospitalized in the respiratory department of a local secondary hospital. On Day -34, she developed type II respiratory failure and underwent endotracheal intubation with ventilator-assisted breathing, after which hypoxemia and CO₂ retention improved. On Day -27, the endotracheal tube was removed, and noninvasive ventilator-assisted ventilation was provided, FiO₂ 0.29, noninvasive ventilator-assisted ventilation IPAP 12cmH₂O EPAP 4cmH₂O. After discharge, the patient's cough, sputum production, and dyspnea further worsened. On the morning of Day -20, because of incoherent speech and abnormal behavior, she was taken by her family to a local psychiatric hospital. That afternoon, she developed urinary incontinence and was unresponsive to calling, without nausea or vomiting, and without limb convulsions, trismus, etc. The next day, she was taken to the emergency department of a local tertiary hospital. Arterial blood gas analysis showed type II respiratory failure. Repeat chest CT showed absorption of left lung consolidation and new lesions in the right lung. Head CT showed no obvious abnormalities. Myasthenia gravis panel and autoimmune encephalitis antibody testing were (-). On Day -10, the patient had severe infection, weak expectoration, and difficulty weaning from the ventilator, and tracheostomy was performed. On Day -7, the patient's condition further worsened, with a decrease in blood pressure, and vasopressor medications were used to maintain blood pressure at about 90/50mmHg. On Day -3, she was transferred to our hospital's emergency department. Past medical history: 13 years status post ovarian cyst surgery; more than 10 years of lumbar disc herniation. Personal history: born in Chongqing; moved to the current place of residence because of marriage. Marital and reproductive history: married at appropriate age; has 1 son, healthy. Family history: parents and younger sister are all healthy; denies family history of hereditary disease. Physical examination: T38.4℃ P 142 beats/min R 18 breaths/min Bp 90/55mmHg. Middle-aged woman, in a sedated state, conscious, poor general condition, able to cooperate with simple commands. Status post tracheostomy, coarse breath sounds in both lungs, with diffuse moist rales. Heart rate 142 beats/min, regular rhythm, no pathologic murmurs heard in any valvular auscultation area. No pitting edema in both lower extremities. Muscle strength grade III in all four extremities, normal muscle tone, bilateral abdominal reflexes, biceps and triceps reflexes, knee and Achilles tendon reflexes normal, Babinski sign (-), meningeal irritation signs (-). At RICU admission: continuous ventilator-assisted ventilation via tracheostomy, A/C mode, f 18 breaths/min, Pi 20cmH₂O, FiO₂ 100%, SpO₂ about 90%, PaO₂ 49.7mmHg, P 142 beats/min, norepinephrine infusion about 0.3ug/kg・min, blood pressure 80-90/40-50mmHg. Ancillary examinations (Day -3): CBC: WBC 14.52*10⁹/L, NEU% 82.9%, Hb 94g/L; liver function: γ-glutamyl transferase 196IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 263IU/L, AST 63IU/L; IL-6: 174.5pg/ml; PCT: 2.85ng/mL; D-Dimer: 5.91ug/mL.

differential_diagnoses.name: Severe bacterial pneumonia (community-acquired pneumonia or hospital-associated pneumonia) with sepsis/septic shock
supporting_evidence: History of fever, cough, expectoration of thick yellow sputum, and dyspnea for more than 50 days, with a maximum body temperature of 39°C
On admission, T 38.4°C, P 142 beats/min, blood pressure 80-90/40-50 mmHg, requiring norepinephrine support, consistent with severe infection with hemodynamic instability.
CBC: WBC 14.52*10⁹/L, NEU% 82.9%; IL-6 174.5 pg/ml, PCT 2.85 ng/mL, supporting bacterial infection and a systemic inflammatory response
Breath sounds are coarse in both lungs, with widespread moist rales audible.

Chest CT images show bilateral pulmonary lesions, predominantly relatively extensive consolidation in the left lower lung/left lung, with newly developed patchy lesions in the right lung, consistent with the imaging features of infectious pulmonary consolidation/bronchopneumonia.
Severe hypoxemia and type II respiratory failure are present, suggesting respiratory failure caused by severe pulmonary infection
opposing_evidence: After anti-infective treatment, the condition did not improve and the disease course was prolonged, suggesting that it may not be simple common bacterial pneumonia or that a special pathogen/noninfectious disease may be present.

differential_diagnoses.name: Aspiration pneumonia
supporting_evidence: The patient previously had incoherent speech, abnormal behavior, unresponsiveness to verbal stimuli, and urinary incontinence, suggesting a risk of aspiration during the period of impaired consciousness
During the course of the disease, repeated intubations were performed, followed by tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation, all of which increased the risk of aspiration and secondary infection.

Chest CT images show consolidative opacities predominantly in the lower lobes and posterior dependent regions, more pronounced in the left lower lung, consistent with the common distribution pattern of aspiration pneumonia
Weak expectoration and difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation, suggesting poor airway protection and sputum clearance ability
opposing_evidence: The initial symptoms began after a cold with cough, yellow sputum, and fever, preceding the occurrence of clearly documented disturbance of consciousness, and the entire clinical course cannot be fully explained by aspiration alone.

differential_diagnoses.name: Atypical pathogen pneumonia or viral pneumonia with secondary bacterial infection
supporting_evidence: There was a history of onset after a "common cold," followed by the gradual development of fever, cough, dyspnea, and wheezing, progressing to severe respiratory failure.
Poor response to anti-infective treatment suggests the possibility of pathogens other than common bacteria or mixed infection.

On the chest CT images, in addition to left lung consolidation, newly developed patchy/ground-glass lesions are also seen in the right lung, which may be seen in viral or atypical pathogen infection with secondary bacterial infection.
During the clinical course, the left lung lesions were absorbed while new lesions appeared in the right lung, suggesting possible lesion migration or polymicrobial infection.
opposing_evidence: Productive cough with thick yellow sputum, elevated white blood cell count and neutrophils, elevated PCT, more suggestive of a bacterial infection phenotype

differential_diagnoses.name: Secondary organizing pneumonia (postinfectious organizing pneumonia)
supporting_evidence: The disease course has been prolonged, and the condition has continued to worsen despite anti-infective therapy and repeated respiratory support.
Repeat chest CT showed resolution of the left lung consolidation and new lesions in the right lung, demonstrating migratory lesions, which can be seen in organizing pneumonia

Chest CT images show patchy bilateral pulmonary consolidation/infiltrates, more prominent in the lower lungs and peripheral/subpleural distribution; the imaging findings may be consistent with organizing pneumonia
Poor response to conventional anti-infective therapy suggests that a non-purely infectious inflammatory response should be considered
opposing_evidence: The patient has high fever, yellow purulent sputum, elevated WBC/NEU, elevated PCT, and manifestations of shock, which more strongly support active infection.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary TB or other chronic specific infections (such as mycobacterial infection)
supporting_evidence: The disease course has been prolonged for more than 50 days, with recurrent worsening despite conventional anti-infective treatment.
Chest CT images show persistent pulmonary consolidation and newly developed lesions in both lungs; chronic atypical infection should be included in the differential diagnosis
A farming lifestyle history suggests long-term environmental exposure, and infection with atypical pathogens cannot be completely excluded.
opposing_evidence: The first-stage information did not mention common accompanying symptoms of TB such as night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis.

Imaging was characterized predominantly by acute consolidation and newly developed patchy opacities; in the first stage, there were no definite findings suggestive of cavitation, tree-in-bud pattern, or upper lobe-predominant distribution.
Elevated PCT and septic shock are more suggestive of severe bacterial infection

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute pulmonary thromboembolism complicated by pulmonary infarction or coexisting with pulmonary infection
supporting_evidence: The patient has severe hypoxemia, and with FiO₂ 100%, PaO₂ was 49.7 mmHg, indicating very severe impairment of oxygenation.
Heart rate 142 beats/min, hypotension, elevated D-dimer 5.91ug/mL; prolonged bed rest, mechanical ventilation, and severe infection are all risk factors for thrombosis.
Some chest CT images may show peripheral patchy lesions; peripheral consolidation may be present in pulmonary infarction.
opposing_evidence: The patient has definite fever, yellow sputum, moist rales, elevated WBC/NEU, and elevated PCT and IL-6, which are more consistent with severe pulmonary infection.
In phase 1, the overall imaging findings are more consistent with bilateral infectious consolidation/infiltration of the lungs rather than an isolated presentation of typical pulmonary embolism.

recommended_exams.exam: Bedside bronchoscopy and lavage fluid mNGS

stage2_input.text: After admission, the patient had persistent fever. Multiple sputum cultures showed extensively drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii. Bedside bronchoscopy was performed, and the lavage fluid was sent for mNGS; sequencing results showed: Acinetobacter baumannii, Corynebacterium striatum, Human herpesvirus 7, Neisseria mucosa, and cytomegalovirus. Bedside echocardiography indicated hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. The ECG showed no typical SⅠQⅢTⅢ pattern, and echocardiography showed that the right ventricle was not enlarged, with a mean pulmonary artery pressure of approximately 30 mmHg.

differential_diagnoses.name: encephalitis
evidence: At disease onset, the patient had fever and psychiatric symptoms.
exclusion_reasons: Physical examination showed no nuchal rigidity or other corresponding signs of intracranial infection.
Head CT at the local hospital showed no abnormalities
Further brain CT and electroencephalogram screening showed no obvious abnormalities
No prior history of stroke-like episodes

differential_diagnoses.name: Severe pneumonia
evidence: At the onset of the disease, the initial presentation was predominantly respiratory symptoms such as cough, sputum production, and fever.
exclusion_reasons: Severe pneumonia commonly presents with type I respiratory failure, but this patient developed type II respiratory failure at onset, and it was difficult to correct.

Chest CT showed that although the lesions involved multiple lobes, they were relatively localized; only Acinetobacter baumannii was cultured as the pathogen, which seems unable to explain the patient's current condition.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary embolism
exclusion_reasons: ECG showed no typical SⅠQⅢTⅢ pattern
Echocardiography showed the right ventricle was not enlarged, and the mean pulmonary artery pressure was approximately 30 mmHg
Pulmonary artery CT could not be completed; pulmonary embolism is not being considered at present.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bedside electromyography showed suspected myogenic damage (slight compression of the deltoid muscle/narrow average motor unit duration).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient presented with cough, sputum production, and dyspnea, but developed type II respiratory failure very early, with repeated intubations, difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation, and weak expectoration; moreover, the extent of lesions on chest CT did not fully match the persistent severe ventilatory failure. At the same time, physical examination showed grade III muscle strength in all four extremities, while head CT, EEG, the myasthenia gravis panel, and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies could not explain the condition, suggesting that the cause should be sought in neuromuscular disease, especially myogenic involvement of the respiratory muscles. Bedside electromyography can preliminarily determine whether the injury is myogenic or neurogenic in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation, help explain respiratory pump failure, narrow the differential diagnosis with encephalitis, simple severe pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, etc., and provide a basis for whether subsequent muscle biopsy and genetic testing are needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further muscle biopsy pathology showed: marked variation in muscle fiber size; numerous scattered basophilic muscle fibers were seen, and multiple muscle fibers contained basophilic vacuoles; MGT staining showed ragged red fibers, accounting for approximately 15%; NADH staining showed 1 whorled muscle fiber, with occasional moth-eaten muscle fibers; COX staining showed more than 70 muscle fibers with loss of enzyme activity; SDH staining showed numerous ragged brown fibers; SDH/COX staining showed a large number of blue fibers; ATP staining showed atrophy of both fiber types, with type I fiber predominance.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Given the patient's long-standing easy fatigability after activity, relatively thin body habitus since childhood, and this presentation characterized by refractory type II respiratory failure and limb weakness, together with EMG findings already suggesting possible myogenic injury, muscle biopsy is needed to directly evaluate muscle fiber architecture and mitochondria-related pathologic changes to determine whether there is a primary myopathy, mitochondrial myopathy, or other metabolic/inflammatory myopathy. The key clinical questions this examination is intended to address are: why severe pneumonia alone cannot fully explain the persistent respiratory muscle weakness and difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation; and whether there is definitive muscle pathologic evidence. Muscle biopsy not only helps confirm mitochondrial myopathy, but also enables pathologic differentiation from inflammatory myopathy, neurogenic muscular atrophy, and others, thereby affecting whether subsequent management should focus on mitochondrial metabolic support, rehabilitation, and long-term ventilatory management, rather than continuing to focus solely on infection or central nervous system disease.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: MGT staining showed ragged red fibers, accounting for approximately 15%;
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has a background of long-standing insidious fatigue and, after infectious stress, developed severe respiratory failure, decreased limb muscle strength, and difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation, suggesting possible decompensation of an underlying metabolic myopathy that was triggered. The purpose of MGT staining is to look for ragged red fibers, an important morphologic clue to mitochondrial proliferation and abnormal aggregation. This test can directly determine whether the patient has characteristic pathologic changes of mitochondrial myopathy, help explain the underlying cause of respiratory and skeletal muscle involvement, and increase diagnostic confidence for mitochondrial disease, providing a basis for further molecular genetic testing and for formulating metabolic supportive treatment such as coenzyme Q10 and L-carnitine.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: NADH staining showed 1 whorled muscle fiber, with occasional moth-eaten muscle fibers;
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In the context of suspected myogenic injury, chronic weakness, and respiratory muscle dysfunction during the critical illness phase, NADH staining is primarily used to assess whether there are abnormalities in oxidative enzyme activity within muscle fibers and in the intermyofibrillar network structure. This examination is intended to determine whether the patient's muscle weakness is accompanied by metabolism-/mitochondria-related structural remodeling, rather than simply disuse weakness or ordinary critical illness myopathy. The identification of whorled fibers and moth-eaten changes helps support abnormalities in intrafiber metabolism and ultrastructure; together with other enzyme stains, it contributes to building the pathologic evidence chain for mitochondrial myopathy and helps exclude some conditions that present only with nonspecific atrophy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: COX staining showed more than 70 enzyme activity-deficient muscle fibers;
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The clinical features of this patient are rapid progression to severe type II respiratory failure and generalized muscle weakness after infection, suggesting that an energy metabolism disorder may be involved in clinical decompensation. COX staining is used to assess enzyme activity related to mitochondrial respiratory chain complex IV, with emphasis on determining whether COX-deficient fibers are present. The clinical question this test is intended to address is whether the muscle involvement is due to a mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation disorder. If a large number of muscle fibers with loss of enzyme activity are identified, this strongly supports a mitochondrial pathophysiologic mechanism and helps reclassify the patient from "respiratory failure caused by infection alone" to "decompensation of underlying mitochondrial myopathy triggered by infection," which is critical for definitive diagnosis and the direction of subsequent metabolic therapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: SDH staining shows numerous fragmented brown muscle fibers;
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had exertional fatigue since childhood and now presents with respiratory muscle weakness; further evaluation of mitochondrial quantity and distribution is needed at the level of muscle enzyme histochemistry. SDH staining reflects mitochondrial-related oxidative enzyme activity and can demonstrate darkly stained fibers caused by abnormal mitochondrial aggregation. This examination is intended to confirm whether there is histologic evidence of mitochondrial proliferation/accumulation and to corroborate findings from MGT, COX, and other results, thereby supporting mitochondrial myopathy rather than simple inflammation, neurogenic lesions, or critical illness-related secondary changes. The results may also help determine the extent and typicality of the lesions and improve the reliability of the pathologic diagnosis.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: SDH/COX staining showed a large number of blue fibers;
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: When the patient already has evidence suggestive of myogenic injury and further confirmation of mitochondrial disease is needed, combined SDH/COX staining can simultaneously assess mitochondrial proliferation and loss of COX enzyme activity, and is an important method for identifying muscle fibers with mitochondrial functional abnormalities. This test is intended to determine whether abnormal muscle fibers show both increased mitochondria and respiratory chain functional defects. A large number of blue fibers suggests COX deficiency with relatively preserved/enhanced SDH, constituting highly valuable evidence for mitochondrial myopathy. It can strengthen the differential diagnosis from other primary myopathies, neurogenic atrophy, and pure critical illness myopathy, and provide strong support for subsequent genetic validation.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: ATP staining showed atrophy of both fiber types, with type I fiber predominance.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has grade III muscle strength in all four extremities, chronically poor exercise tolerance, and severe difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation. It is necessary to determine the muscle fiber type distribution and atrophy pattern to assess whether there is selective fiber involvement, disuse change, or features consistent with a primary myopathy. ATP staining can distinguish type I and type II muscle fibers and help clarify the pathologic basis of muscle weakness and whether the atrophy has a specific pattern. Although this test alone is not sufficient to definitively diagnose mitochondrial myopathy, when combined with other enzyme stains and routine pathology, it can provide a more comprehensive assessment of the nature of muscle involvement, help exclude purely neurogenic injury or nonspecific muscle atrophy caused by prolonged bed rest, and provide reference value for rehabilitation training and assessment of expected recovery of respiratory muscle function.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: First-generation sequencing analysis found that the patient's peripheral blood sample carried a mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) A3243G point mutation, with a mutation rate of 66%.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient’s history includes exertional fatigue since childhood and a thin body habitus. During this episode, after infectious stress, the patient again developed type II respiratory failure, limb weakness, and difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation that could not be fully explained by the pulmonary lesions alone. Electromyography suggested myogenic injury, and muscle biopsy together with multiple enzyme stains also supported a mitochondria-related disorder; therefore, genetic testing is needed to complete etiologic confirmation. The core clinical question of first-generation sequencing analysis is whether a known pathogenic mtDNA mutation is present to definitively establish mitochondrial myopathy. Detection of the A3243G point mutation and a high mutation rate can not only confirm the diagnosis and exclude other nonhereditary myopathies, but also has implications for disease classification, prognostic assessment, family genetic counseling, and shifting the subsequent treatment focus from anti-infective therapy alone to mitochondrial metabolic support and long-term rehabilitation management.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further head CT and EEG screening showed no obvious abnormalities.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: During the course of the illness, the patient developed central nervous system symptoms including incoherent speech, abnormal behavior, unresponsiveness to verbal stimuli, and urinary incontinence. In the setting of severe infection and respiratory failure, acute intracranial structural lesions must first be ruled out, such as intracerebral hemorrhage, cerebral infarction, and significant encephalitis/cerebral edema, in order to avoid missing reversible or life-threatening causes. Although the final clinical impression was more suggestive of respiratory muscle involvement due to mitochondrial myopathy, the role of head CT was to rapidly assess whether the psychiatric and behavioral abnormalities were caused by obvious structural brain abnormalities and to help exclude differential diagnoses such as stroke. The negative result provided a stronger clinical basis for shifting attention to metabolic/myopathic causes, rather than attributing the respiratory failure and altered consciousness entirely to an acute intracranial emergency.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further head CT and EEG screening showed no obvious abnormalities.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient previously had abnormal behavior and was unresponsive to verbal stimuli, but had no definite typical convulsive manifestations such as limb jerking or jaw clenching. EEG is still needed to assess whether there is nonconvulsive status epilepticus, diffuse cerebral dysfunction, or encephalitis-related electrographic changes. The clinical question this test aims to address is whether the psychiatric symptoms and altered consciousness are due to abnormal cortical discharges or impaired brain parenchymal function. In the context of a negative head CT, if EEG shows no obvious abnormalities, this would help reduce the likelihood of diagnoses such as encephalitis and epileptic events, supporting that these manifestations are more likely related to severe infection, respiratory failure, or decompensation associated with underlying mitochondrial disease, thereby avoiding deviation in the treatment direction.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: A detailed history was obtained. The patient has felt fatigued after activity since childhood, has a relatively thin body habitus, and has done relatively little farm work or other labor. Bedside electromyography showed suspected myogenic injury (deltoid muscle with mildly reduced recruitment/shortened mean motor unit duration). Further muscle biopsy pathology showed marked variation in muscle fiber size, with many scattered basophilic muscle fibers and basophilic vacuoles within multiple muscle fibers; MGT staining showed ragged red fibers, accounting for approximately 15%; NADH staining showed 1 whorled muscle fiber and occasional moth-eaten muscle fibers; COX staining showed more than 70 muscle fibers with absent enzyme activity; SDH staining showed many ragged brown fibers; SDH/COX staining showed a large number of blue fibers; ATP staining showed atrophy of both fiber types, with type I fiber predominance. First-generation sequencing analysis found that the patient's peripheral blood sample carried the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) A3243G point mutation, with a mutation rate of 66%. Further screening with brain CT and EEG showed no obvious abnormalities.

diagnostic_basis: Since childhood, the patient has felt fatigued after physical activity and has had a relatively thin body habitus.
Physical examination: muscle strength in all four extremities Grade III
Bedside electromyography showed suspected myogenic injury
Muscle biopsy pathology showed ragged red fibers, muscle fibers with loss of enzyme activity, etc.
First-generation sequencing analysis identified a mitochondrial DNA A3243G point mutation.

treatment_plan: Treatment with high-dose idebenone, coenzyme Q10, levocarnitine, arginine, taurine, vitamin B1, and vitamin B2
Biofeedback therapy, muscle rehabilitation training, and other treatments
Rehabilitation therapy, intermittent use of noninvasive ventilator
treatment_response: The patient was gradually weaned off mechanical ventilation, and muscle strength in all four extremities gradually recovered.
4 months after discharge, the patient was able to ambulate and was independent in activities of daily living.
